who: Deaf and hard of hearing people
People in noisy places or on mute
People working in a second language
People who need to read along to follow speech
takeaways: Live video with sound, such as webinars, livestreams and town halls, has captions in real time. Level AA.
Live captions are usually typed by a trained human captioner or made by speech recognition. Accuracy matters: a wrong name or number is wrong information.
It covers video with sound. Live audio with no video, like a live radio show, is 1.2.9. Once the recording is published, it is prerecorded and needs captions under 1.2.2.
Designers own the event plan and the player: booking captions in time, where they appear, the control to show them, and space so they do not cover slides.
failures: Captions that only appear on the replay
Only the host’s microphone captioned, not guests or audience questions
check: In the event plan, confirm who provides captions and that they are booked before the date.
In the player design, check captions show without covering slides, names or the speaker.
In a rehearsal, mute the stream and follow the whole session from captions alone, including guests and questions.

quiz.question: Your company runs a quarterly all-hands livestream. Budget is tight. What meets 1.2.4?
options: A captioned recording published the next day
The slide deck shared before the event
Captions shown in real time during the stream
quiz.why: Live viewers need the words while it is happening. A captioned recording helps later viewers under 1.2.2, and slides do not carry what people say.

spec: Show where live captions appear in the player and the event page, and the control to turn them on.
Note the caption provider, how their text reaches the stream, and the names and terms to send them in advance.
Reserve space in the layout so captions never cover slides, names or the chat.
review: Who is captioning this, and are they booked?
Are guest speakers and audience questions captioned too?
What happens to the recording and its captions afterwards?
tradeoff: Human captioners cost more than automatic captions but handle names, accents and jargon far better. Book a human for high-stakes events. For routine streams, test automatic captions with your own vocabulary and check people can really follow them.
system: Make captions on by default in your livestream template and player, with a caption area reserved in the layout.
pitch: If someone cannot hear the town hall, they did not attend it. Live captions put them in the room.
